## LLM Recipe

### 1.2 Model Architecture &amp; Scaling Laws

#### [Multi-View MoE: Letting Every Router Shape Expert Computation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40577>)

Multi-View MoE combines several routers to choose experts, then reuses each expert’s router preferences to blend learned input representations before a single expert evaluation. This improves the tested latent-space mixture-of-experts model’s quality with a fixed active-expert budget, while adding routing and projection work.

**Published:** 2026-10-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-30T10:08:26.369Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Mixture of Experts, Routing, Latent Representations

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.40577v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 20-page v1 inspected, including Algorithm 1 and Appendices A–B. In matched 708B-token training, the 10B-total/1B-active model’s nine-task mean rises from 33.07 to 34.25 with 0.19% extra parameters. Controlled mixing interventions support expert- and token-dependent input use. This unreported October 30 reserve received full review today; earlier discovery time is preserved.

**Limitations:** Main comparisons share one training seed; some tasks regress. Output-norm correlation is a utility proxy. Expert FLOPs and dispatch volume stay fixed, but total compute does not; measured throughput covers other ablation variants. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

### 1.3 Pretraining &amp; Optimization

#### [Your LR Schedule May Not Be Principled: Effective Learning Rate Scheduling in Weight-Normalized Training](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.40362>)

This study links weight-normalized training gains to the learning rate relative to parameter norms, and proposes an affine inverse-square-root schedule called AIR. Matching effective learning-rate trajectories largely aligns the tested normalization and weight-decay loss curves, providing a practical way to compare training recipes and design their annealing schedules.

**Published:** 2026-10-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-30T10:08:26.631Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Effective Learning Rate, Learning Rate Schedules, Weight Normalization, MoE Pretraining

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/pdf/2610.40362v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Complete 25-page v1 and proof assumptions inspected. With matched warmup, terminal and cumulative learning rates, AIR lowers evaluation loss 1.843→1.832 and raises the eleven-task average 56.22→57.78 on a 790M-active/35.7B-total MoE trained 500B tokens. A smaller 128B-token study and late-stage interventions support the mechanism. Editorial catch-up retains the actual October 30 first-seen time.

**Limitations:** Terminal summaries are single trajectories, not seed confidence intervals; tuning budgets differ and some tasks regress. Theory assumes fixed-direction, tangential constant-statistics dynamics and does not prove global loss optimality. Norm replay is partly retrospective. No author implementation or independent reproduction was verified.

## AI Agent Dev

### 2.3 Context Engineering &amp; Memory

#### [CALM: Conflict-Aware Lifecycle Memory Governance for Long-Horizon Language Agents](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.38573>)

CALM preserves superseded memories for historical questions while controlling which records enter an agent’s current reasoning context. Deterministic lifecycle rules track conflicts and dependencies, and a separate fixed or learned gate admits evidence according to the query, helping avoid stale but semantically relevant context.

**Published:** 2026-10-28 · **First seen:** 2026-10-30T03:08:56.616-07:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Memory Governance, Temporal Reasoning, Evidence Selection

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.38573v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections 3–4 and Appendices A–B: with Qwen3-30B-A3B on all 500 LongMemEval-S questions, accuracy is 79.60%, versus 77.20% for validity reranking and 76.60% for fixed gating. CALM variants share cached top-48 retrieval and nominal memory budgets; learned admission uses separate development supervision. Results also cover 1,540 non-adversarial LoCoMo questions with three answer models. Editorial catch-up from the October 30 abstract reserve, preserving the original October 28 paper date.

**Limitations:** One fixed seed; external baselines retain different native pipelines. Development-set size and several gate-training hyperparameters are unspecified. Rule coverage, upstream retrieval and automatic judges constrain conclusions; no author implementation was verified. Appendix B.7 contains inconsistent robustness arithmetic, excluded from this summary.

### 2.5 Agent Learning &amp; Skill Acquisition

#### [Compile Away Uncertainty: Self-Evolving Agent Skills via Programmatic Compilation](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39508>)

SkillCompiler turns well-specified operations within evolving agent skills into locally validated programs while retaining language-model reasoning for context-dependent decisions. A persistent program bank reuses compatible implementations across skills, reducing repeated procedural generation without updating model weights.

**Published:** 2026-10-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-31T10:04:16.682+00:00 · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Agent Skills, Program Compilation, Execution Reliability

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.39508v1>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Sections III–V and the operational appendix: across three independently learned banks, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash reaches 98.26% success on 134 ALFWorld tasks, versus 93.53% for the strongest reported baseline. A separate fixed-bank LiveMath experiment repeats 100 tasks three times: mixed success/failure outcomes fall from SkillOpt’s 32% to 11%. Persistent banks are frozen before testing, although task-local program synthesis remains allowed. This is an unreported October 30 original-batch paper discovered in the lookback, not an October 31 release.

**Limitations:** Development included inspection of held-out failures. Local validation does not prove correctness for all inputs; evolution budgets differ and token/call savings are not uniform. No author code release was verified, and dynamic open-world robustness is unestablished.

## AI Training &amp; Inference Infra

### 3.3 Inference Engines &amp; Serving

#### [PDScope: Breaking the Prefill-Decode Seesaw for Memory-Bound MoE Inference](<https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.39216>)

PDScope uses different expert prediction and CPU/GPU placement policies for prefill and decode, coordinating the current layer with predicted demand in the next. Cost-guided prefetching and streamlined execution reduce the conflict between GPU compute utilization and PCIe traffic in memory-constrained local MoE inference.

**Published:** 2026-10-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-30T10:09:08.628Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** MoE Offloading, Phase-Aware Scheduling, CPU GPU Inference

[Paper](<https://arxiv.org/html/2610.39216v1>) · [Code](<https://github.com/nezha-Anonymous/PDScope>)

**Evidence:** research-paper; full-text. Read all 15 pages, Algorithm 1 and released reference implementation. Four BF16 MoEs run on A100/Intel 6230R and RTX 3090/EPYC 7452 systems with GPU memory capped at 24 GB, ShareGPT prompts of 128–4096 tokens and 64 outputs, averaging ten runs. Versus MoE-APEX, reported maxima are 2.5× prefill and 2.1× decode throughput. This is editorial catch-up after October 30 discovery; the original October 29 paper date is retained. Repository history also starts October 29, but commit clocks do not prove exact public visibility.

**Limitations:** Gains are phase-throughput maxima, not universal end-to-end speedups. Profiling/training costs under 30 minutes per model are excluded from inference throughput; prefill/decode overlap is unsupported. No downstream-quality evaluation is supplied. Released code substitutes a gate-fallback predictor and covers one Qwen3 single-request setup on a different CPU, without the paper’s learned predictor or comparative baseline suite.

#### [Day 0 support for Mistral Large 4 on vLLM](<https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4>)

vLLM’s Mistral Large 4 report explains how cross-layer KV sharing, context parallelism and sparse-attention communication compose with graph execution and speculation. Its measurements show when extra KV capacity helps long sessions and when communication overhead makes ordinary tensor parallelism faster.

**Published:** 2026-10-29 · **First seen:** 2026-10-30T10:09:08.769Z · **Novelty:** newly-discovered · **Tags:** Context Parallelism, KV Sharing, Sparse Attention, Serving Tradeoffs

[Blog](<https://vllm.ai/blog/2026-10-29-mistral-large-4>) · [Code](<https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm>) · [Project](<https://recipes.vllm.ai/mistralai/Mistral-Large-4-1T-A52B>)

**Evidence:** engineering-report; full-text. Full publisher Markdown, linked recipe and relevant PR changes inspected. On eight GB300s, NVFP4 DCP8 expands KV capacity from 3.60M to 28.76M tokens. A separate TP8 DCP8 FP8 comparison with 60K-input/1K-output requests and no speculation combines communication changes and decode fusions: at concurrency 64, output throughput rises 139.1→204.0 tokens/s. October 29 is the report date; earlier October 12/26/27 PRs establish older implementation. October 30 discovery is preserved as catch-up, without an exact first-public timestamp.

**Limitations:** DCP8 is 16–28% slower per token than ordinary TP8 when capacity does not bind. KV capacity is not validated million-token serving; the recipe validates up to 256K. Combined optimization gains do not isolate each change. Speculation consumes capacity; several components remain open PRs, and full model support requires dedicated images rather than a release/nightly wheel. No universal speedup or cross-hardware ranking is established.
